definition_citations.quote:
A compact **Type I region** is

$$D=\{(x,y):a\le x\le b,\ \alpha(x)\le y\le\beta(x)\},$$

where $a<b$, the continuous piecewise-$C^1$ functions $\alpha,\beta$ satisfy $\alpha\le\beta$, and $\alpha<\beta$ on $(a,b)$. A compact **Type II region** is defined analogously by continuous piecewise-$C^1$ functions $\lambda\le\rho$ on $[c,d]$:

$$D=\{(x,y):c\le y\le d,\ \lambda(y)\le x\le\rho(y)\}.$$

An **elementary Green region** admits both descriptions. By [[thm-fubini-over-a-region-between-continuous-graphs]], each Type I description is compact and Jordan measurable.

A **finite elementary Green region** is a nonempty finite union $D=D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_N$ of elementary Green regions with pairwise disjoint interiors. Pairwise intersections must be finite unions of complete shared boundary arcs and endpoints, and every positive-length internal arc must belong to exactly two pieces with opposite induced orientations. This supplied decomposition is part of the data; it is not inferred from an arbitrary closed curve.

For a Type I region of [[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]], the **positive boundary** traverses the lower graph from left to right, the right endpoint arc upward, the upper graph from right to left, and the left endpoint arc downward, omitting zero-length arcs. For a Type II description it traverses the right graph upward, the top endpoint arc from right to left, the left graph downward, and the bottom endpoint arc from left to right. In both cases the region remains locally on the left.

For a finite elementary Green region, delete every shared internal arc together with its oppositely oriented copy and retain the orientations of all surviving arcs. Reversal and concatenation are those of [[def-piecewise-c1-path-operations-and-oriented-reparametrizations]].

The surviving arcs form a finite list $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ of oriented piecewise-$C^1$ arcs, called the **positive boundary chain** $\partial D$. A finite elementary Green region need not be connected and need not be simply connected, so this list need not assemble into a single closed path. Accordingly, for a continuous field $G$ on a neighbourhood of $D$ the boundary integral is defined as the finite sum

$$\int_{\partial D}G\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{k=1}^m\int_{\sigma_k}G\cdot d\mathbf r,$$

and likewise $\int_{\partial D}P\,dx+Q\,dy$ for the field $(P,Q)$. When the surviving arcs do assemble into one closed path — in particular for a single elementary region, whose positive boundary is the concatenation of its four arcs — this sum is that path's integral, because vector line integrals add under concatenation ([[thm-line-integrals-under-reversal-and-concatenation]]). The value is independent of the order of the list, since a finite sum of reals does not depend on its order.

A **compact Jordan parameter region** is a compact Jordan measurable set $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ that is the closure of its nonempty connected interior $D^\circ$ ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]). Its boundary has content zero ([[thm-jordan-boundary-criterion]]).

A regular parametrized surface patch is the image of a $C^1$ map from a compact Jordan parameter region whose parameter cross product is nonzero on the region's interior and for which no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of the whole region. Seam identifications and rank failures may occur only on the boundary. Here $C^1$ is the Euclidean componentwise class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. More precisely, the parametrization $\varphi$ is defined on an open neighbourhood of $D$, $\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\ne0$ on $D^\circ$, and no point of $D^\circ$ has the same image as a distinct point of $D$. The chosen pair $(D,\varphi)$ is part of the patch data.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Adopt as physical postulates of this framework, on the spacetime and particle
model of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and
[[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]] and on the special-relativity particle
model [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]:

(i) [Test charge in a prescribed external field] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ be a
constant charge parameter ([[def-em-sources]]), $m>0$ an externally supplied
rest mass, $x:J\to A$ a future timelike $C^2$ massive worldline with
four-velocity $U$, and let $F$ be a prescribed field of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] that is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the graph
of $x$ and is generated externally to the particle. Adopt the equation of
motion

$$m\,\frac{dU}{d\tau}=q\,\Phi(U),$$

where, at each original parameter $s\in J$, $\Phi=\Phi_{x(s)}$ is the
raised-index operator of the field at $x(s)$, defined by
$\eta(\Phi_{x(s)}(u),w)=F(x(s))(w,u)$
([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]); equivalently
$m\,dU^\mu/d\tau=q\,F^{\mu\nu}U_\nu$. Here $dU/d\tau$ is the derivative of $U$
with respect to its proper-time function $\tau(s)$: explicitly
$dU/d\tau=U'(s)/\tau'(s)$, with
$\tau'(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}>0$. It is the four-acceleration of the worldline
([[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]). The particle's own field
is excluded from $F$: this is the external-field coupling, and it defines no
self-force.

(ii) [Continuum matter coupling] For a smooth source $(\rho,J)$ of
[[def-em-sources]] interacting with the field through an explicitly stated
matter model to which this coupling applies, adopt the force density
$\rho E+J\times B$ (unit N m$^{-3}$) and the power density $J\cdot E$ (unit
W m$^{-3}$) as the electromagnetic source terms of that matter model, with the
spatial cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; they describe the local
interaction of the field with matter and are not a property of a prescribed
current alone.

(iii) [Scope] The rest mass and the charge are inputs; $m$ is not derived within
electromagnetism. The coupling is adopted for constant $q$ and $m>0$; no
magnetic-monopole coupling, no radiation reaction and no self-force are
included. In particular the nonrelativistic coordinate statement
$mr''=q(E+r'\times B)$ is not adopted as exact: the adopted statement is the
covariant one of clause (i), and any low-speed statement requires its own
approximation hypotheses and error bounds.

Let the laboratory region, its inertial chart and the fields and sources be those
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], with the
units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; fix the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the chart and the oriented volume form $\varepsilon$ of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], with $\varepsilon_{0123}=+1$ and
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$.

(a) [Components] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, define the
covariant components of the **electromagnetic two-form** $F$ in the chart by
$F_{00}=0$, $F_{0i}:=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}:=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$
($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) and $F_{ab}:=-F_{ba}$, the index-raised components being
$F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Here
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the spatial permutation symbol of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]. Then $F$ is a $C^k$ type-$(0,2)$
tensor field on $U$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], alternating at every event, and the
components above are exactly its component functions: at $p\in U$ the tensor
$F(p)$ is the bilinear form $F(p)(u,w)=F_{ab}(p)u^aw^b$ on $V$ in the
coordinates $u^a,w^b$ of $u,w$ in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Indeed each $F_{ab}$ is
a finite sum of products of the $C^k$ functions $E_i,B_k$ of the chart
coordinates with the constants $c,\epsilon_{ijk}$, hence a $C^k$ function of
$x(p)$, and the component criterion of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]] applies.

(b) [Observer decomposition] Let $n:=e_0$ be the future unit timelike vector of
the chart and let $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$ be the observer
components of [[thm-sr-antisymmetric-observer-decomposition]]; then
$e_i=+E_i/c$, $b_i=-B_i$ and $e_0=b_0=0$, and the invariants and square wedge
of that theorem read

$$\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2,\qquad F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=+4\,(E\cdot B)/c,\qquad F\wedge F=-2\,(E\cdot B)\,\varepsilon/c,$$

where $|\cdot|$ and $\cdot$ are the spatial Euclidean structure of the frame.
(For the same pair $(E,B)$, that theorem's optional clause (d) uses
$F_{\rm optional}^{i0}=E_i/c$ and $F_{\rm optional}^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, so
$F_{\rm optional}=-F$ in all six components, not only the magnetic block. This
framework fixes clause (a) and uses the theorem's general algebra; its optional
SI dictionary must be converted by negating the entire tensor.)

(c) [Potentials when they exist] If $\varphi$ and $A$ are $C^1$ with
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, and
$A^\mu:=(\varphi/c,A)$, $A_\mu:=\eta_{\mu\nu}A^\nu$, then
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$; conversely, if a $C^1$
covector field $A_\mu$ on $U$ satisfies $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu
-\partial_\nu A_\mu$, then $E,B$ recovered from $F$ by clause (a) obey
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ with
$\varphi:=-cA_0$ and the spatial potential vector $A:=(A_1,A_2,A_3)$. Here
$\nabla$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] in the spatial coordinates,
and the spatial cross-product conventions of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] are
used. The definition does not assert that every field pair admits such a
potential; where a $C^1$ potential represents the $C^1$-or-better field of
clause (a), the field is closed in the explicit sense
$\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}=0$. This conclusion does not require second
classical derivatives of the potential: put
$H_{\lambda\mu\nu}:=\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}$, which is continuous because $F$ is $C^1$; for
every smooth compactly supported test $\psi$, substituting $F=dA$ and
integrating by parts twice, moving the derivatives first onto $\psi$
([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]] (b)) and then off the
potential factors after commuting only the smooth test derivatives
([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]), gives $\int H\psi=0$; the
fundamental lemma (a) of [[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]
then gives $H=0$. The framework's potential theorems establish existence only
under their stated hypotheses; [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]
supplies the coordinate derivatives $\partial_\mu$ used throughout.

(d) [Four-current and index-raising operator] With the adopted four-current
$j=(c\rho,J)$ of [[def-em-sources]], the raised-index operator $\Phi$ of
[[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]], defined pointwise on $V$ by
$\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$, satisfies
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$; the components of $F$
carry the tesla (T), those of $j$ carry A m$^{-2}$, and those of a
four-potential $A^\mu$ carry T m.

The particle and light objects of the framework are the following curves and
vector fields of the affine Minkowski model ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]],
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), with the physical interpretation of
[[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and the units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Worldlines] A **worldline** is a regular causal curve $x:J\to A$ in one of
the regularity classes of [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] ($J$ an
order-convex subset of $\mathbb R$ with at least two elements). A **massive
worldline** is a $C^k$ future timelike worldline, $k\ge1$, with everywhere
nonzero future timelike tangent. A **future null curve** is a $C^1$ curve with
everywhere nonzero future null tangent. An **ideal vacuum light ray** of the
adopted physical model follows a null straight line: on its parameter interval
it has the form $x(s)=p+\lambda(s)v$, where $p\in A$, $v\in V$ is nonzero
future null, and $\lambda$ is $C^1$ with $\lambda'(s)>0$. This is the
straight-ray adoption of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]]; arbitrary
future null curves are retained as kinematic objects without asserting that
they describe vacuum light propagation. Along a null curve the integrand
$-\eta(x',x')$ of the proper-time construction
([[def-sr-proper-time]]) vanishes identically, so that construction yields no
proper-time parametrization of it, and a light ray is never treated as a
massive worldline. A worldline is a curve in spacetime; its reading $r\circ x$
in a named laboratory chart is a coordinate description of it, not an object of
another observer.

(b) [Four-velocity and four-acceleration] For a massive worldline the
four-velocity $U$ and, when it is $C^2$, the four-acceleration $A$ are those of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]; wherever defined they satisfy
$\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $\eta(U,A)=0$, by
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

(c) [Chart reading] If a massive $C^2$ worldline is described in a laboratory
chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] by $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ on an open interval of
laboratory times, then $|r'(t)|<c$ for every $t$, with four-velocity
$U=\gamma(c,r')$ and Lorentz factor
$\gamma=(1-|r'|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, by clause (e) of
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

(d) [Frames and observers] An inertial frame in this framework is the
origin-with-basis object of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]; a point
observer is a future unit timelike vector $n\in V$ with rest space $n^\perp$ and
rest projection $h$, as in clauses (c)-(d) of
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. On an open spacetime region
$W\subseteq A$, an **observer congruence field** means a $C^1$ map $n:W\to V$ with
$n(p)$ future timelike and $\eta(n(p),n(p))=-1$ at every $p$; its observer
histories, when given, are integral curves satisfying $dx/d\tau=cn(x)$.
A **tetrad field** is a tuple of $C^1$ maps $(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3):W\to V^4$
whose values form a positively oriented $\eta$-orthonormal basis at every
event, with $f_0$ future timelike. Regularity here means componentwise $C^1$
in inertial coordinates. These fields need not be constant and are distinct
from an inertial origin-with-basis frame, its coordinate chart and a single
point observer; no global congruence or tetrad is asserted to exist.

(e) [Scope] No force law, no self-field and no extended-body structure is
supplied here; an accelerating massive worldline requires a force model stated
separately, and an ideal light ray carries no dispersive, quantum or
polarisation structure in this definition.

Let $c > 0$ and let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the dimensionless four-velocity lies on the future unit
hyperboloid $\{v \in C^{+}:\eta(v,v)=-1\}$.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = (0,w)$ in the frame coordinates, identified with $w$ via the spatial basis.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be nonempty and open and $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open interval, with the laboratory frame, fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, units and $c>0$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) A **moving material circuit** is data $(D,r,v)$. The nonempty compact parameter set $D=D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_N\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ has a supplied finite elementary Green decomposition, including the opposite orientations on shared arcs, as in [[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]]. Its positive boundary chain $\partial D=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)$ is the finite list of surviving oriented piecewise $C^1$ arcs after internal pairs cancel ([[def-positive-orientation-for-elementary-region-boundaries]]). The map $r:D\times I\to\Omega$ extends to a $C^2$ map on an open neighbourhood of $D\times I$, has $r_u\times r_w\ne0$ on $D^\circ\times I$, and is injective on $D$ at each time. These conditions are the meaning of an embedded material sheet here. Its **swept spacetime graph** is $\mathcal G:=\{(r(p,t),t):p\in D,\ t\in I\}\subseteq\Omega\times I$. A compatible **material velocity** is a $C^1$ map $v:W\to\mathbb R^3$ on an open $W\subseteq\Omega\times I$ containing $\mathcal G$, satisfying $v(r(p,t),t)=r_t(p,t)$. Thus coincident images must have the same velocity. Material labels are the points $p=(u,w)\in D$.

(b) Put $S(t):=r(D,t)$ and $\gamma_t:=(r(\cdot,t)\circ\sigma_k)_{k=1}^m$, a boundary **chain**, whose trace is $C(t):=r(\partial D,t)$. We use $\partial S(t)$ for this parametrized boundary chain, rather than the ambient topological boundary of the subset $S(t)\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. A finite Green region can have several components or holes, so $\gamma_t$ need not be one closed path. For $B$ jointly $C^1$ on a spacetime neighbourhood of $\mathcal G$, the **magnetic flux** is

### Well-definedness and conventions

Each $D_i$ is compact and Jordan measurable; its boundary has content zero. The finite union $D$ is Jordan measurable, and its continuous flux integrand is Riemann integrable by [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. At a fixed time each elementary piece is an admissible regular $C^2$ patch: its interior is connected and dense in that piece, the parameter cross product is nonzero there, and injectivity prevents interior image identifications ([[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]]). All integrals over the full sheet mean the sum over the pieces, with internal boundary arcs cancelling. Neither connectedness nor a single boundary loop is assumed for their union.

Composition of each $\sigma_k$ with the $C^2$ slice gives a piecewise $C^1$ path. Its trace lies in the time-$t$ slice of $W$, where $E+v\times B$ is continuous, so each line integral exists. The chain sum is independent of its ordering. Spatial derivatives of two $C^2$ extensions agreeing on $D\times I$ agree first on $D^\circ\times I$ by difference quotients and then on its closure in each time slice by continuity; since $I$ is open the same argument gives the time derivative. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]). In the setting of [[def-em-moving-patch]]: $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a finite elementary Green region with positive boundary chain $\partial D$, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval, $r:D\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ extends to a $C^2$ map on a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ with $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on $D^\circ\times I^\circ$, $(W,v)$ is a $C^1$ velocity field with $v(r(p,t),t)=r_t(p,t)$, and $B$ is a $C^1$ field on an open set containing the swept graph $\Sigma=\{(r(p,t),t):p\in D,t\in I\}\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, with flux

$$\Phi(t)=\int_D\bigl\langle B(r(p,t),t),\,r_u(p,t)\times r_v(p,t)\bigr\rangle\,dp .$$

For nondegenerate $I$, $\Phi$ is differentiable at interior times and relatively differentiable at included endpoints. Empty $I$ gives no flux values, and singleton $I$ gives one flux value but no derivative determined by that value. If the spatial divergence $\operatorname{div}B=0$, then for every time of such a nondegenerate $I$ whose slice has rank two, that is $r_u(p,t)\times r_v(p,t)\ne0$ for all $p\in D^\circ$,

$$\Phi'(t)=\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB\cdot n\,dS-\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r .$$

By the standing hypothesis the slice has rank two at every interior time. At an included endpoint the displayed normal notation is used only if its slice also has rank two. Here $S(t)$ means the parametrized family $(D,r(\cdot,t))$, and $n$ means the parameter normal $N(p,t)=(r_u\times r_v)/\lVert r_u\times r_v\rVert_2$ on $D^\circ$. Define $\int_{S(t)}H\cdot n\,dS:=\int_D\langle H(r(p,t),t),r_u\times r_v\rangle\,dp$, including multiplicity; similarly $\int_{S(t)}(v\cdot n)\operatorname{div}B\,dS:=\int_D\langle v(r(p,t),t),r_u\times r_v\rangle\operatorname{div}B(r(p,t),t)\,dp$. These agree with the ordinary flux definitions when the slice meets [[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]] (through [[def-em-moving-patch]]); no image-wide normal or injectivity is assumed. If $\partial D=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)$, define $\oint_{\partial S(t)}G\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{\ell=1}^m\int_{r(\sigma_\ell,t)}G(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r$ using [[def-positive-orientation-for-elementary-region-boundaries]] and [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]. Without the hypothesis $\operatorname{div}B=0$ the additional term

$$\int_{S(t)}(v\cdot n)\,\operatorname{div}B\,dS$$

appears on the right-hand side. The identity is local in $t$ and is a statement about the parametrized mathematical object; no electromagnetic interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention
already carried by the imported finite piecewise $C^1$ boundary presentations
and by the compact $C^1$ surface measure cited below
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ open and
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open interval. This definition fixes the
time-independent spatial test geometries of the integral form of the Maxwell
equations.

(a) [Volume test geometry] A **volume test geometry** in $\Omega$ is a pair
$(V,\nu_V)$ where $V\subseteq\Omega$ is a nonempty bounded open set with
$\overline V\subseteq\Omega$ and a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation
of its boundary ([[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]), and
$\nu_V$ is the outward unit normal of that presentation off its edge set
([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]). The
**closed-surface flux** of a field $F$ continuous on a neighbourhood of
$\overline V$ is the finite face sum

$$\oint_{\partial V}F\cdot\nu_V\,dS:=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_V\,dS,$$

with the face surface integrals of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. For every closed
axis-parallel box $K=\prod_{i<3}[a_i,b_i]\subseteq\Omega$ with $a_i<b_i$, its
open interior $V=\prod_{i<3}(a_i,b_i)$ is a volume test geometry and
$\overline V=K$; its natural six-face presentation is the boundary of $K$, with
outward normals $\pm e_i$. The volume variable is $V$, while $K$ denotes its
compact closure. Each face is a degenerate three-dimensional box and hence has
$\lambda_3$-measure zero by
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]; their finite union
$K\setminus V$ is null. Thus for continuous $h$ on a neighbourhood of $K$,
$\int_Vh\,d\lambda_3=\int_Kh\,d\lambda_3$: the positive and negative integrals
over the null difference vanish by
[[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]] and
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]].

(b) [Patch test geometry] A **patch test geometry** in $\Omega$ is a regular
$C^2$ surface patch $(D,r)$ over a finite elementary Green region in the sense
of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]]
([[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]],
[[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]]): $D\subseteq\mathbb
R^2$ is a finite elementary Green region, $r$ is of class $C^2$ on an open
neighbourhood of $D$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]),
$r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on the interior of $D$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]) and
no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of $D$. Its
**induced boundary chain** $\partial S=r(\partial D)$ and its **circulation**
$\oint_{\partial S}F\cdot d\mathbf r$ for a field continuous on the image are
those of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]]
([[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]); its
**oriented flux** of a field $F$ continuous on the image is

$$\int_SF\cdot n_S\,dS:=\int_D(F\circ r)\cdot(r_u\times r_v)\,dudv,$$

the scalar Riemann integral of the continuous integrand on the compact Jordan
parameter region, in the orientation induced by $r$
([[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]). The pair $(D,r)$
is part of the data. Every affine graph patch $r(u,v)=(u,v,\varphi(u,v))$ over
an axis-parallel square $D=[c_1,c_1+\ell]\times[c_2,c_2+\ell]$ with $\ell>0$,
whose graph lies in $\Omega$ with $\varphi$ affine (for instance constant), and
more generally every affine regular patch over such a square, is a patch test
geometry: the square is a finite elementary Green region, and $r$ is smooth and
regular with $\varphi_u,\varphi_v$ constant.

(c) [Regularity convention] When an integral identity of this framework is
asserted for a volume test geometry $V$, respectively for a patch test geometry
$S$, with respect to a field $F$ of stated class $C^k$, it concerns fields
defined and of class $C^k$ on an open neighbourhood of $\overline V$ in
$\Omega$, respectively of the image $r[D]$ in $\Omega$; when the identity
involves a time derivative of a flux, the field is defined with the stated
regularity on a neighbourhood of that compact set times the compact time
interval of the assertion. No regularity away from these neighbourhoods is
asserted.

(d) [Conventions and scope] Test geometries are fixed spatial subsets of
$\Omega$ and carry no motion. A patch's orientation is the one induced by its
parametrization, and its induced boundary chain has the compatible orientation
of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]], so that the
classical Stokes theorem applies with a plus sign. The definition retains the
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of the imported boundary and surface-measure
definitions; it asserts no differential equation, no physical law and no
existence of fields.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of the
imported piecewise $C^1$ boundary and surface-measure definitions
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; let
$E,B$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and $\rho,J$ source fields of
[[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$; and let $(V,\nu_V)$ and $(D,r)$ be the
volume and patch test geometries of [[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]]. Assume the
fields are jointly $C^1$ on $\Omega\times I$ and that the additional
derivatives appearing below exist and are continuous there; for instance $E,B$
jointly of class $C^2$ and $\rho,J$ of class $C^1$ is sufficient.

(a) [Differential implies integral] If the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, then for every
volume test geometry $(V,\nu_V)$ and every $t\in I$,

$$\oint_{\partial V}E(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\int_V\rho(\cdot,t)\,d\lambda_3,\qquad \oint_{\partial V}B(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS=0,$$

and for every patch test geometry $(D,r)$ the flux functions
$t\mapsto\int_SB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ and
$t\mapsto\int_SE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ are differentiable on $I$ and, for
every $t\in I$,

$$\oint_{\partial S}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=-\frac{d}{dt}\int_SB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS,\qquad \oint_{\partial S}B(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=\mu_0\int_SJ(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS+c^{-2}\frac{d}{dt}\int_SE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS.$$

(b) [Integral implies differential] Conversely, suppose the two volume
identities of (a) hold for every volume test geometry and every $t\in I$, and
that for every patch test geometry the two flux functions are differentiable
on $I$ and the two patch identities of (a) hold for every $t\in I$. Then the
four smooth-branch equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] hold pointwise on
$\Omega\times I$:

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

The equivalence is asserted for the exact class of test geometries of
[[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]], which contains the open interiors of all closed
axis-parallel boxes compactly contained in $\Omega$ and the affine square
patches; it is not a recovery from one selected volume or one selected patch,
and the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the time derivative of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] are the operators used.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial

the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the

presupposed here.

[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Adopt as physical postulates of this framework, on the spacetime and particle
model of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and
[[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]] and on the special-relativity particle
model [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]:

(i) [Test charge in a prescribed external field] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ be a
constant charge parameter ([[def-em-sources]]), $m>0$ an externally supplied
rest mass, $x:J\to A$ a future timelike $C^2$ massive worldline with
four-velocity $U$, and let $F$ be a prescribed field of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] that is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the graph
of $x$ and is generated externally to the particle. Adopt the equation of
motion

$$m\,\frac{dU}{d\tau}=q\,\Phi(U),$$

where, at each original parameter $s\in J$, $\Phi=\Phi_{x(s)}$ is the
raised-index operator of the field at $x(s)$, defined by
$\eta(\Phi_{x(s)}(u),w)=F(x(s))(w,u)$
([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]); equivalently
$m\,dU^\mu/d\tau=q\,F^{\mu\nu}U_\nu$. Here $dU/d\tau$ is the derivative of $U$
with respect to its proper-time function $\tau(s)$: explicitly
$dU/d\tau=U'(s)/\tau'(s)$, with
$\tau'(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}>0$. It is the four-acceleration of the worldline
([[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]). The particle's own field
is excluded from $F$: this is the external-field coupling, and it defines no
self-force.

(ii) [Continuum matter coupling] For a smooth source $(\rho,J)$ of
[[def-em-sources]] interacting with the field through an explicitly stated
matter model to which this coupling applies, adopt the force density
$\rho E+J\times B$ (unit N m$^{-3}$) and the power density $J\cdot E$ (unit
W m$^{-3}$) as the electromagnetic source terms of that matter model, with the
spatial cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; they describe the local
interaction of the field with matter and are not a property of a prescribed
current alone.

(iii) [Scope] The rest mass and the charge are inputs; $m$ is not derived within
electromagnetism. The coupling is adopted for constant $q$ and $m>0$; no
magnetic-monopole coupling, no radiation reaction and no self-force are
included. In particular the nonrelativistic coordinate statement
$mr''=q(E+r'\times B)$ is not adopted as exact: the adopted statement is the
covariant one of clause (i), and any low-speed statement requires its own
approximation hypotheses and error bounds.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ be piecewise-$C^1$. If $a=b$, define both line integrals below to be $0$. If $a<b$, choose an admissible partition $a=t_0<\cdots<t_m=b$ and a continuous derivative extension $v_i$ on each piece. Let $f$ be a continuous scalar field and $F$ a continuous vector field on a set containing the trace of $\gamma$. The **scalar line integral with respect to arc length** and the **vector-field line integral** are

$$\int_\gamma f\,ds:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}f(\gamma(t))\lVert v_i(t)\rVert_2\,dt,$$

$$\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}\langle F(\gamma(t)),v_i(t)\rangle\,dt,$$

where the inner product is [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The summands exist by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. Independence of the admissible partition is proved in [[lem-line-integrals-are-independent-of-the-piecewise-c1-partition]].

**Set form.** Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, let $a<b$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function, defined and continuous together with its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

and at $t=a$ and $t=b$ it has relative (one-sided) derivatives, taken within $[a,b]$, both equal to the same displayed integral. Equivalently, for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$,

$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{h_k}\Bigl(\int_Kf(x,t+h_k)\,d\lambda_n(x)-\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\Bigr)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$

**Surface form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. Let $S$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, and let $f$ be real-valued, defined and continuous together with $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$ is differentiable in the same relative sense with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)=\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma).$$

The statements are pointwise in $t$ and make no claim about moving parameter sets $K(t)$ or $S(t)$, about singularities crossing $K$ or $S$, about differentiability of $\partial_tf$, or about differentiation in the spatial variables; only the one-dimensional parameter $t$ is differentiated. Integrals are Lebesgue integrals, and the surface integrals are those of the cited surface measure; the case $K=\varnothing$ or $\lambda_n(K)=0$ is included and the two sides vanish.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $Q=\prod_{i=1}^n[a_i,b_i]$ with $n\ge1$ and $a_i<b_i$. If a bounded Borel real function $f$ on $Q$ is Riemann integrable, then it is Lebesgue integrable and the two integrals agree. The corresponding assertion for complex functions holds componentwise. In particular it applies to smooth compact test integrands and their bounded Borel zero extensions from compact Jordan regions.

Let $(D,\varphi)$ be a $C^2$ patch over a finite elementary Green region ([[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]]), with positive boundary chain $\partial D=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)$ and induced boundary chain $\varphi(\partial D)$, and let $F$ be a $C^1$ vector field on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ containing $\varphi[D]$. Then the circulation around the induced boundary chain equals the flux of the curl in the induced orientation:

$$\oint_{\varphi(\partial D)}F\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_D\bigl\langle(\operatorname{curl}F)\circ\varphi,\ \varphi_u\times\varphi_v\bigr\rangle.$$

The right-hand side is the flux of $\operatorname{curl}F$ through the patch in the orientation induced by $\varphi$, in the sense of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

For a Type I region of [[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]], the **positive boundary** traverses the lower graph from left to right, the right endpoint arc upward, the upper graph from right to left, and the left endpoint arc downward, omitting zero-length arcs. For a Type II description it traverses the right graph upward, the top endpoint arc from right to left, the left graph downward, and the bottom endpoint arc from left to right. In both cases the region remains locally on the left.

For a finite elementary Green region, delete every shared internal arc together with its oppositely oriented copy and retain the orientations of all surviving arcs. Reversal and concatenation are those of [[def-piecewise-c1-path-operations-and-oriented-reparametrizations]].

The surviving arcs form a finite list $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ of oriented piecewise-$C^1$ arcs, called the **positive boundary chain** $\partial D$. A finite elementary Green region need not be connected and need not be simply connected, so this list need not assemble into a single closed path. Accordingly, for a continuous field $G$ on a neighbourhood of $D$ the boundary integral is defined as the finite sum

$$\int_{\partial D}G\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{k=1}^m\int_{\sigma_k}G\cdot d\mathbf r,$$

and likewise $\int_{\partial D}P\,dx+Q\,dy$ for the field $(P,Q)$. When the surviving arcs do assemble into one closed path — in particular for a single elementary region, whose positive boundary is the concatenation of its four arcs — this sum is that path's integral, because vector line integrals add under concatenation ([[thm-line-integrals-under-reversal-and-concatenation]]). The value is independent of the order of the list, since a finite sum of reals does not depend on its order.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$. Then $F\times G$ is $C^1$ on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(F\times G)=\langle\operatorname{curl}F,G\rangle-\langle F,\operatorname{curl}G\rangle,$$

$$\operatorname{curl}(F\times G)=(\operatorname{div}G)F-(\operatorname{div}F)G+DF\,G-DG\,F.$$

Here $DF\,G$ denotes the map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ whose $i$th coordinate at $p$ is $\sum_{j<3}\partial_jF_i(p)\,G_j(p)$, that is, the Jacobian matrix of $F$ at $p$ applied to the vector $G(p)$, and $DG\,F$ is defined the same way with the roles of $F$ and $G$ exchanged. The operators are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], the cross product is that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], the inner product that of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the Jacobian matrix that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

derivations.claim: Write $a=r_u\times r_w$ and $h(p,t)=\langle B(r(p,t),t),a(p,t)\rangle$. These functions have continuous time derivatives on a neighbourhood of $D\times I$. Fix any $t\in I$ and a compact nondegenerate time interval around it contained in $I$; [F14], with the Riemann/Lebesgue comparison on a bounding rectangle, gives $\Phi_B'(t)=\int_D\partial_th\,dp$. Put $M=D_xv$. Compatibility and [F16] give $\partial_t r_u=Mr_u$, $\partial_t r_w=Mr_w$. The elementary determinant identity $\det[Mq_0,q_1,q_2]+\det[q_0,Mq_1,q_2]+\det[q_0,q_1,Mq_2]=\operatorname{tr}(M)\det[q_0,q_1,q_2]$ follows by expanding in the three columns and checking the standard-basis triples (repeated indices cancel; distinct indices give the trace). With $q_0=B$, $q_1=r_u$, $q_2=r_w$ it yields $\langle B,\partial_ta\rangle=\langle (\operatorname{div}v)B-MB,a\rangle$. Thus [F16] gives $\partial_th=\langle\partial_tB+(D_xB)v+(\operatorname{div}v)B-(D_xv)B,a\rangle=\langle\partial_tB+v\operatorname{div}B-\operatorname{curl}(v\times B),a\rangle$. Here all spatial derivatives are at fixed laboratory time on the open time slice of $W\cap(\Omega\times I)$. Since $\operatorname{div}B=0$ by [F9], integrating and applying [F15] on each elementary piece, then cancelling oppositely oriented internal arcs, gives $\Phi_B'(t)=\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB\cdot n\,dS-\oint_{\gamma_t}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r$. Parameter integrals add over the pieces because they have disjoint interiors and null boundaries; [F14] transfers this finite Lebesgue additivity to the Riemann integrals. This argument applies at every $t\in I$.

Fix $t\in K$. Every elementary $D_i$ is the closure of its nonempty connected interior, hence is a compact Jordan parameter region. The frozen restriction of $r$ is $C^2$, has nonzero parameter cross product on that interior, and is injective, so it is a patch test geometry of [F4]. Apply [F5] to each such fixed spatial patch, differentiating its flux with respect to a separate field time $s$ and evaluating at $s=t$. Sum the resulting identities and cancel internal arcs as in [F15]. This gives $\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS=-\oint_{\gamma_t}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r$. The separate variable $s$ keeps this fixed-patch derivative distinct from the moving flux derivative.

On each arc of $\gamma_t$, additivity of the Euclidean pairing [F11] and Riemann integral linearity [F12] split the line integral of $E+v\times B$ into those of $E$ and $v\times B$; summing the arcs gives $\mathrm{emf}=\oint_{\gamma_t}E\cdot d\mathbf r+\oint_{\gamma_t}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r$ by [F2] and [F13]. Substitution of step 1.2 into step 1.1 proves $\mathrm{emf}(t)=-\Phi_B'(t)$ for every $t\in K$.

The claimed differentiability, transport formula, elementary-piece test geometries, fixed-patch Faraday formula and emf identity follow from steps 1.1–2.1. The transport identity agrees with the general parametrized formula of [F3]. The additional subluminal external-test-charge reading is the local coordinate-force calculation of [[def-em-moving-circuit-geometry]](c) from [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](i); it does not replace relativistic momentum by $mv$ and is unused in the integral algebra. Countable Choice is carried through the comparison and Maxwell interfaces. The regular fields and compact swept graph on $D\times K$ exclude singularity crossings. No empirical or full matter-dynamical assertion is made.
