citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Adopt the following reduced circuit model in the laboratory frame and SI units of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]. The continuum material reference is [[post-em-material-closure]]; the terminal laws below are additional assumptions, rather than consequences of its pointwise constitutive relations or of Maxwell's equations.

(a) **Branch data.** Fix a nonempty interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, a finite set of nodes $\mathcal N$, and a finite set of oriented branches $\mathcal E$, each with specified tail and head nodes. Designate $n$ inductive/resistive branches, $m$ capacitive branches and any source branches. On the first family specify currents $I:J\to\mathbb R^n$ and separate voltage-drop vectors $V_L,V_R:J\to\mathbb R^n$; on the second specify charges $Q:J\to\mathbb R^m$, currents $I_C:J\to\mathbb R^m$ and voltage drops $V_C:J\to\mathbb R^m$. Currents $I$ and charges $Q$ admit $C^1$ extensions to an open interval containing $J$; included endpoint derivatives are their one-sided derivatives, and at a singleton the chosen extensions are part of the data supplying the jets. Voltages and source currents are continuous. The matrices $L,R\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and $C\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ are constant, with $L^{\mathsf T}=L$, $C^{\mathsf T}=C$, $z^{\mathsf T}Cz>0$ for every $z\ne0$, $R^{\mathsf T}=R$, and $y^{\mathsf T}Ry\ge0$ for every $y$. These inequalities define positive definiteness and positive semidefiniteness here. Symmetry alone is imposed on a declared $L$; a smooth compact-current realization can supply its additional positivity. Geometry, orientations and source data are fixed.

(b) **Element and network relations.** Adopt
$$V_L=L\dot I,\qquad V_R=RI,\qquad I_C=\dot Q,\qquad V_C=C^{-1}Q.$$
Positive definiteness makes $C^{-1}$ well defined: $Cz=0$ implies $z^{\mathsf T}Cz=0$, hence $z=0$; an injective square finite matrix is invertible by [[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]]. The voltage drop on an inductive/resistive branch is $(V_L+V_R)_\alpha$, with either element omitted by setting its corresponding matrix to zero; a capacitive branch has drop $(V_C)_\beta$. Thus the three voltage symbols refer to distinct element drops. In a purely inductive use, abbreviate $V_L$ by $V$. The linkage is $LI$ and the induced emf convention is $e_L:=-V_L$. The capacitor scalar law is $V_C=Q/C$ when $m=1$.

For a branch $b$ let $i_b$ be its oriented current and $v_b$ its voltage drop from tail to head (a source may have a negative drop). Define the incidence matrix by $A_{ab}:=\mathbf1_{\{a=\operatorname{tail}(b)\}}-\mathbf1_{\{a=\operatorname{head}(b)\}}$. **Kirchhoff's current law** is $Ai(t)=0$, expressing no node-charge accumulation. A **closed walk** is a finite sequence of traversals of branches with matching successive nodes and final node equal to initial node. If its signed traversal count is $z_b$ (forward minus backward), **Kirchhoff's voltage law** is $\sum_bz_bv_b(t)=0$. Adopt it for every closed walk. Equivalently it suffices to impose it on a chosen linearly independent spanning set (basis) of the real span of their traversal-count vectors; this is the meaning of independent loops here. These are imposed ideal network constraints, not statements about arbitrary field circulations.

The bookkeeping energies are $\frac12I^{\mathsf T}LI$ and $\frac12Q^{\mathsf T}C^{-1}Q$. If a smooth compact conserved-profile realization of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b) is specified, identification of its linkage matrix with the declared $L$ is an additional model premise, not automatic.

(c) **Quasistatic regime.** Specify a geometric size $\ell>0$, a time scale $T>0$ and a chosen dimensionless tolerance $0<\epsilon_{\rm qs}<1$. The declaration $\ell/(cT)\ll1$ means $\ell/(cT)\le\epsilon_{\rm qs}$ with a tolerance regarded as small in the chosen application. Negligible radiation and leakage, ideal terminals and the fixed conductor geometry are separately adopted idealizations. Neither this inequality nor these idealizations give a quantitative error bound for an arbitrary full Maxwell solution; no universal accuracy is asserted.

(d) **Units and scope.** $V_L,V_R,V_C,v_b$ carry volts, $I,I_C,i_b$ amperes, $Q$ coulombs, $t$ seconds, $L$ henries ($\mathrm H=\mathrm V\,\mathrm s\,\mathrm A^{-1}$), $C$ farads ($\mathrm F=\mathrm C\,\mathrm V^{-1}$), and $R$ ohms ($\Omega=\mathrm V\,\mathrm A^{-1}$). The model excludes radiation, distributed-element, nonlinear, hysteretic, leakage and proximity effects; resistor loss is retained through $R$. Subluminal material speeds are required if a relativistic moving-matter interpretation is added. The model is adopted and contains no measurement or derivation from the vacuum Maxwell equations.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

**Why this item is first.** The published definition of the integral does not
cover this page. [[def-darboux-integral]] is stated for reals $a < b$, because
the partitions it quantifies over are those of [[def-partition-and-refinement]],
whose standing hypothesis is $a < b$: with $a = b$ the chain
$a = t_0 < \dots < t_n = b$ is unsatisfiable. So $\int_a^b f$ is an undefined
symbol whenever $a \ge b$, and every additivity statement below would be
ill-formed as it is usually written. This item extends the notation, and nothing
else: the object it names is still the Darboux integral of
[[def-darboux-integral]].

Let $u, v \in \mathbb{R}$ and write

$$[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v] \;:=\; \text{the closed interval with endpoints } u \text{ and } v$$

([[def-interval]]). Let $f$ be a real-valued function whose domain contains that
interval. Say that **$f$ is integrable between $u$ and $v$** when either $u = v$,
or $u \ne v$ and the restriction of $f$ to $[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v]$ is bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux integrable there ([[def-darboux-integral]],
[[def-darboux-sums]]). For such $f$ define

$$\int_u^v f \;:=\; \begin{cases} \text{the Darboux integral of } f \text{ over } [u,v] & \text{if } u < v, \\[2pt] 0 & \text{if } u = v, \\[2pt] -\displaystyle\int_v^u f & \text{if } u > v. \end{cases}$$

**There is nothing to check for consistency.** The three clauses are indexed by
the three cases of trichotomy, $u < v$, $u = v$ and $u > v$, which are mutually
exclusive and exhaustive; no pair of them ever applies to the same $(u,v)$. In
particular the first clause is untouched, so on $u < v$ this is the published
integral verbatim and every published theorem about it applies unchanged.

**The middle clause is a stipulation, not a computation.** It is *not* claimed
that $0$ is a value forced by the $u < v$ definition in any limiting sense; that
definition simply says nothing at $u = v$, and $\int_u^u f := 0$ is what is
written there. It is also unconditional: no hypothesis on $f$ beyond being
defined at $u$ is asked for, since the case $u = v$ never refers to a partition.

### The two consequences used throughout the page

**Antisymmetry, for every pair.** For all reals $u, v$ with $f$ integrable
between them,

$$\int_u^v f \;=\; -\int_v^u f .$$

Indeed if $u < v$ then $v > u$ and the third clause reads
$\int_v^u f = -\int_u^v f$, which rearranges to the display; if $u = v$ both
sides are $0$; and if $u > v$ the third clause is the display itself.

**Absolute values agree.** Consequently
$\bigl|\int_u^v f\bigr| = \bigl|\int_v^u f\bigr|$ for every such pair.

**An obligation recorded here and discharged elsewhere.** With this convention
the additivity identity

$$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f$$

holds for **every** arrangement of $u, v, w$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable, not only for $u < v < w$. That is a theorem and not part of this
definition; it is proved as the last clause of
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], and nothing on this page uses it before it
is proved there.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $j_1,\dots,j_n\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}j_\alpha=0$ be fixed compact smooth conserved current profiles of the class of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b), extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. Fix amplitudes $I\in\mathbb R^n$, put $J_I:=\sum_{\alpha=1}^nI_\alpha j_\alpha$, let $A_{J_I}$ be the Coulomb-gauge Newtonian vector potential of [[pthm-em-magnetostatic-vector-potential]] applied to the conserved current $J_I$, and let $B_{J_I}=\operatorname{curl}A_{J_I}$. Define the linkage coefficients
$$L_{\alpha\beta}:=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\langle j_\alpha(x),j_\beta(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x),\qquad\alpha,\beta=1,\dots,n .$$
The amplitudes $I_\alpha$ carry amperes and the profiles $j_\alpha$ are shapes per unit current, with units $\mathrm m^{-2}$; their numerical SI maps belong to the stated smooth class. Consequently $J_I$ has unit $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$, $A_{J_I}$ has $\mathrm T\,\mathrm m$, $L_{\alpha\beta}$ has H, the linkage has Wb and $U$ has joules. $A_{j_\alpha}$ denotes the linear potential response per ampere. Then:

(a) [Finiteness and self-energy] every $L_{\alpha\beta}$ is a finite real number: the defining double integral converges absolutely, and in particular every self-coefficient $L_{\alpha\alpha}$ is finite, so the compact smooth profiles carry a finite self-energy. This is a statement about the smooth profiles only; no finite value is assigned to a zero-radius thin-wire self-inductance.

(b) [Reciprocity and flux linkage] $L_{\alpha\beta}=L_{\beta\alpha}$ for all $\alpha,\beta$; $A_{J_I}=\sum_{\alpha}I_\alpha A_{j_\alpha}$ componentwise; and for every $\beta$ the linkage integral is
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle j_\beta,A_{J_I}\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\sum_{\alpha=1}^nL_{\beta\alpha}I_\alpha .$$
Thus the numbers $L_{\alpha\beta}$ are the linkage coefficients of the profiles: the linkage of profile $\beta$ with the field of the superposition is the linear combination $\sum_\alpha L_{\beta\alpha}I_\alpha$.

(c) [Magnetic energy and positivity] with $U(I):=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J_I,A_{J_I}\rangle\,d\lambda_3$,
$$U(I)=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta=1}^nL_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha I_\beta=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J_I}|^2\,d\lambda_3\ \ge0,$$
all quantities finite; moreover $U(I)=0$ holds precisely when $J_I=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$. Consequently the symmetric matrix $L=(L_{\alpha\beta})$ is positive semidefinite, and it is positive definite exactly when the profiles are pointwise linearly independent, i.e. when $\sum_\alpha I_\alpha j_\alpha\equiv0$ forces $I=0$.

(d) [Scope] the theorem concerns fixed compact smooth conserved current profiles and their Coulomb-gauge fields. It asserts no thin-wire, sheet or singular self-inductance; no time-dependent, moving, radiating or material configuration; and no uniqueness of the vector potential. The identification of these coefficients with the inductance matrix of the adopted lumped circuit model, and of the linkage derivatives with terminal voltages, is adopted in [[post-em-circuit-approximation]]; the strict material-loop theorem applies separately only to an actual moving sheet and compatible smooth Maxwell fields satisfying its hypotheses. No terminal-voltage law for arbitrary varying frozen profiles is inferred from the present magnetostatic computation.

For the Lebesgue/surface/distributional source and admissibility branches (c)-(d), assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The smooth formulation in (a) and the smooth conserved-current predicate in (b) do not themselves use Choice. Let the laboratory region and its chart, the field and source objects and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and fix $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

**(a) [Steady-current regime].** A steady-current (magnetostatic) configuration on $\Omega\times I$ consists of a field pair $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and source fields $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that are independent of $t$ and satisfy the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For such a configuration the formal distributional branch of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] gives $\operatorname{div}J=0$ distributionally; this is pointwise when $J$ is $C^1$. In the jointly $C^2$ field/$C^1$ source branch its classical proof applies directly. The locally integrable distributional reading here inherits Countable Choice, whereas the stated classical $C^2/C^1$ compatibility calculation is choice-free, and the four adopted equations are equivalent to the electrostatic pair and the magnetostatic pair
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J .$$

**(b) [Compact smooth current class].** The compact smooth current class of this framework consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. A magnetostatic field of such a current is a field $B$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with the extended $J$. This is the hypothesis class of the vector-potential, Biot-Savart and dipole theorems of this page; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of $B$ in the class.

**(c) [Ideal source objects].** Define three ideal current source objects outside the compact class, together with the data selecting their fields. Curve parameters $s$ and $L$ and the radius $a$ carry metres; the signed line-current amplitude $I$ carries amperes and the signed sheet-current amplitude $K$ carries A m$^{-1}$. The field $B$ carries tesla, as in [[def-em-si-conventions]].

**(c1) [Closed thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ ($L>0$) and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal loop current is the distribution
$$\langle J_\gamma,\psi\rangle:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),$$
with $\rho_\gamma:=0$.

**(c2) [Infinite straight wire].** For $\gamma(s)=(0,0,s)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal wire current is
$$\langle J_{\rm w},\psi\rangle:=I\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_3(0,0,s)\,ds,$$
with $\rho_{\rm w}:=0$.

**(c3) [Infinite cylindrical sheet].** For $a>0$, $S=\{\rho=a\}$, $\rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$, $e_\rho:=\rho^{-1}(x_1,x_2,0)$ and $e_\varphi:=\rho^{-1}(-x_2,x_1,0)$ on $\{\rho>0\}$, and $K\in\mathbb R$, the ideal solenoid sheet current is
$$\langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=K\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$$
([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], read on compact cylinder segments), with $\rho_S:=0$. All three pairings are finite because $\psi$ has compact support.

**(c4) [Admissibility].** A field $B$ is admitted for one of these declared models when: $B$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$ (hence a distribution by [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $C^1$ off the support of the current; $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ hold pointwise off that support; the distributional identities $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold against every scalar divergence test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and vector curl test $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ in the sense of [[def-distributional-derivative]]; $B$ has the model's declared symmetry: in (c2) and (c3), $B(x+he_3)=B(x)$ for every $h\in\mathbb R$, and $B(R_\theta x)=R_\theta B(x)$ for every $\theta\in\mathbb R$, at off-source points, where $R_\theta(x_1,x_2,x_3)=(x_1\cos\theta-x_2\sin\theta,x_1\sin\theta+x_2\cos\theta,x_3)$; no symmetry is required in (c1); and $B$ obeys the decay requirement: $|B(x)|\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ in (c1), and in (c2), (c3), $\sup_{(\theta,z)\in C}|B(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z)|\to0$ as $r\to\infty$ for every nonempty compact $C\subset\mathbb R^2$. The companion examples exhibit and verify the fields of the two axisymmetric models in this class; the definition itself asserts no existence, uniqueness, finite energy or limiting relation for the declared models, and no compact-class theorem of this page applies to them.

**(d) [Scope].** This is a model restriction: the steady-current regime for compact smooth currents, and three explicitly declared ideal noncompact or singular models. It excludes point charges, weaker-regularity volume sources, moving sheets, normal sheet currents and any claim of empirical exactness; the equations in (c4) define a mathematical admissibility predicate; its physical adoption for these source objects is a separate postulate, and no product of distributions is formed.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: Fix the $C^1$ extension of $I$ to an open interval $U\supseteq J$, and define $W(y):=\frac12\langle y,Ly\rangle=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}y_\alpha y_\beta$ for $y\in\mathbb R^n$, so that $t\mapsto G(t):=W(I(t))=\frac12\langle I(t),LI(t)\rangle$ is the bookkeeping-energy function of the Statement. For each pair $(\alpha,\beta)$ the product $t\mapsto I_\alpha(t)I_\beta(t)$ is differentiable on $U$ with derivative $\dot I_\alpha I_\beta+I_\alpha\dot I_\beta$ by [F3], and $G$ is a finite linear combination of these products; applying the sum and scalar rules of [F3] repeatedly therefore gives, for every $t\in J$, $$G'(t)=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}\bigl(\dot I_\alpha(t)I_\beta(t)+I_\alpha(t)\dot I_\beta(t)\bigr)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}\dot I_\alpha(t)I_\beta(t)=\langle L\dot I(t),I(t)\rangle=\langle V(t),I(t)\rangle ,$$ where the second equality relabels $\alpha\leftrightarrow\beta$ in one half of the sum and uses the symmetry $L_{\alpha\beta}=L_{\beta\alpha}$, and the last two use [F10] and $V=L\dot I$; the derivative $G'$ is continuous on $J$, being a finite sum of products of continuous functions.

Assume now the realization hypotheses of clause (b). For each fixed $t\in J$ put $J_I(t):=\sum_\alpha I_\alpha(t)j_\alpha$, a member of the compact smooth conserved class; applying [F7] to the amplitudes $I(t)=(I_1(t),\dots,I_n(t))$ (its coefficients are the linkage numbers of the profiles $j_1,\dots,j_n$, which by hypothesis coincide with the entries of $L$) gives $$\frac12\langle I(t),LI(t)\rangle=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha(t)I_\beta(t)=U(I(t))=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J_I(t),A_{J_I(t)}\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J_I(t)}|^2\,d\lambda_3\ \ge0 ,$$ the outer equalities by [F10] and the definition of $U$ in [F7]; this is clause (b)'s energy identity at each fixed $t$.

Let $u:=\min\{t_0,t_1\}$ and $v:=\max\{t_0,t_1\}$; then $[u,v]\subseteq J$, since $J$ is order-convex by [F2] and contains both $u$ and $v$. If $u<v$, then $G$ is differentiable at every point of $[u,v]$ as a function on $[u,v]$ (interior points lie in the open set $U$, and at $u,v$ the one-sided derivatives exist by restriction of the extension), while $G'$ is continuous on $[u,v]$ by step 1.1 and hence integrable there by [F4]; [F5] gives $\int_u^vG'=G(v)-G(u)$, that is $\int_u^v\langle V,I\rangle=G(v)-G(u)$ by step 1.1. If $u=v$ the same display is $0=G(v)-G(u)$, which holds identically and is the $u=v$ reading of [F6]. If $t_0>t_1$, applying the already-proved case to the pair $(t_1,t_0)$ and the sign clause of [F6] gives $\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\langle V,I\rangle=-\int_{t_1}^{t_0}\langle V,I\rangle=-(G(t_0)-G(t_1))=G(t_1)-G(t_0)$. In every case $\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\langle V(t),I(t)\rangle\,dt=\frac12\langle I(t_1),LI(t_1)\rangle-\frac12\langle I(t_0),LI(t_0)\rangle$, which is the identity of (a); for $n=1$ the quadratic form is $\frac12LI^2$ by [F10].

Combining steps 2.1 and 1.2 gives, for all $t_0,t_1\in J$, $$\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\langle V(t),I(t)\rangle\,dt=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J_I(t_1),A_{J_I(t_1)}\rangle\,d\lambda_3-\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J_I(t_0),A_{J_I(t_0)}\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J_I(t_1)}|^2\,d\lambda_3-\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J_I(t_0)}|^2\,d\lambda_3 ,$$ so that the accumulated terminal energy is the change of the frozen field energy, as asserted in (b). The terminal law $V=L\dot I$ is the adopted branch relation [F1], and the identification of the model's inductance matrix with the linkage matrix is the additional realization hypothesis of (b), not a consequence of the magnetostatic theorem alone.

Clause (c) holds as stated: the computation is fixed-geometry bookkeeping of the adopted model; changing geometry would add the mechanical work term, and the frozen realization is not asserted to solve any time-dependent Maxwell system. Units are those of [F9]; the singleton case of (a) was handled in step 2.1, where the extension supplies the derivative and no intrinsic derivative is inferred from the value restriction. Countable Choice enters only through clause (b), inherited from the linkage theorem [F7] and its Newtonian and measure interfaces; clause (a) is choice-free.

boundaries.evidence: The index set may be empty ($n=0$): then $I$ maps to $\mathbb R^0$, $V=L\dot I=0$, the finite sums of step 1.1 are empty and give $G\equiv0$, and step 1.2 gives $0=0$; clause (b) with the zero profile has $U=0$ by [F7].

For $I\equiv0$ the terminal voltage $V=L\dot I\equiv0$, step 1.1 gives $G'\equiv0$, step 2.1 gives $\int\langle V,I\rangle=0=G(t_1)-G(t_0)$, and step 1.2 with the zero instantaneous source gives $U(0)=0\ge0$.

For $n=1$ and $L>0$, step 2.1 reads the quadratic form as $\frac12LI^2$ and step 3.1 gives the field-energy difference; the scalar case is the displayed reading of clause (a) and no special value of any counting parameter occurs.
$L$ need not be invertible: steps 1.1-2.1 use only symmetry $L_{\alpha\beta}=L_{\beta\alpha}$, and step 1.2 obtains $U\ge0$ from [F7] for every amplitude, including those in the kernel of $L$.

For $t_0,t_1\in J$ step 2.1 covers $t_0<t_1$ by [F5], $t_0=t_1$ by [F6], and $t_0>t_1$ by [F6]'s sign clause with the already-proved case; derivatives at included endpoints are read through the open-neighbourhood extension of the Statement.
Countable Choice is used only in clause (b), inherited from [F7]'s Newtonian and measure interfaces, as steps 1.2 and 4.1 record; clause (a) and the algebra of steps 1.1-3.1 are choice-free.
The only equivalence invoked is [F7]'s criterion $U(I)=0\iff J_I=0$, quoted and used in step 1.2; the item asserts no equivalence of its own and its terminal identity is an equality of numbers.

There is no converse direction in the item: the identity $\int\langle V,I\rangle=\Delta\frac12\langle I,LI\rangle$ is proved for all pairs $t_0,t_1$ in step 2.1 and is symmetric under exchanging $t_0,t_1$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Adopt the following reduced circuit model in the laboratory frame and SI units of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]. The continuum material reference is [[post-em-material-closure]]; the terminal laws below are additional assumptions, rather than consequences of its pointwise constitutive relations or of Maxwell's equations.

(a) **Branch data.** Fix a nonempty interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, a finite set of nodes $\mathcal N$, and a finite set of oriented branches $\mathcal E$, each with specified tail and head nodes. Designate $n$ inductive/resistive branches, $m$ capacitive branches and any source branches. On the first family specify currents $I:J\to\mathbb R^n$ and separate voltage-drop vectors $V_L,V_R:J\to\mathbb R^n$; on the second specify charges $Q:J\to\mathbb R^m$, currents $I_C:J\to\mathbb R^m$ and voltage drops $V_C:J\to\mathbb R^m$. Currents $I$ and charges $Q$ admit $C^1$ extensions to an open interval containing $J$; included endpoint derivatives are their one-sided derivatives, and at a singleton the chosen extensions are part of the data supplying the jets. Voltages and source currents are continuous. The matrices $L,R\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and $C\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ are constant, with $L^{\mathsf T}=L$, $C^{\mathsf T}=C$, $z^{\mathsf T}Cz>0$ for every $z\ne0$, $R^{\mathsf T}=R$, and $y^{\mathsf T}Ry\ge0$ for every $y$. These inequalities define positive definiteness and positive semidefiniteness here. Symmetry alone is imposed on a declared $L$; a smooth compact-current realization can supply its additional positivity. Geometry, orientations and source data are fixed.

(b) **Element and network relations.** Adopt
$$V_L=L\dot I,\qquad V_R=RI,\qquad I_C=\dot Q,\qquad V_C=C^{-1}Q.$$
Positive definiteness makes $C^{-1}$ well defined: $Cz=0$ implies $z^{\mathsf T}Cz=0$, hence $z=0$; an injective square finite matrix is invertible by [[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]]. The voltage drop on an inductive/resistive branch is $(V_L+V_R)_\alpha$, with either element omitted by setting its corresponding matrix to zero; a capacitive branch has drop $(V_C)_\beta$. Thus the three voltage symbols refer to distinct element drops. In a purely inductive use, abbreviate $V_L$ by $V$. The linkage is $LI$ and the induced emf convention is $e_L:=-V_L$. The capacitor scalar law is $V_C=Q/C$ when $m=1$.

For a branch $b$ let $i_b$ be its oriented current and $v_b$ its voltage drop from tail to head (a source may have a negative drop). Define the incidence matrix by $A_{ab}:=\mathbf1_{\{a=\operatorname{tail}(b)\}}-\mathbf1_{\{a=\operatorname{head}(b)\}}$. **Kirchhoff's current law** is $Ai(t)=0$, expressing no node-charge accumulation. A **closed walk** is a finite sequence of traversals of branches with matching successive nodes and final node equal to initial node. If its signed traversal count is $z_b$ (forward minus backward), **Kirchhoff's voltage law** is $\sum_bz_bv_b(t)=0$. Adopt it for every closed walk. Equivalently it suffices to impose it on a chosen linearly independent spanning set (basis) of the real span of their traversal-count vectors; this is the meaning of independent loops here. These are imposed ideal network constraints, not statements about arbitrary field circulations.

The bookkeeping energies are $\frac12I^{\mathsf T}LI$ and $\frac12Q^{\mathsf T}C^{-1}Q$. If a smooth compact conserved-profile realization of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b) is specified, identification of its linkage matrix with the declared $L$ is an additional model premise, not automatic.

(c) **Quasistatic regime.** Specify a geometric size $\ell>0$, a time scale $T>0$ and a chosen dimensionless tolerance $0<\epsilon_{\rm qs}<1$. The declaration $\ell/(cT)\ll1$ means $\ell/(cT)\le\epsilon_{\rm qs}$ with a tolerance regarded as small in the chosen application. Negligible radiation and leakage, ideal terminals and the fixed conductor geometry are separately adopted idealizations. Neither this inequality nor these idealizations give a quantitative error bound for an arbitrary full Maxwell solution; no universal accuracy is asserted.

(d) **Units and scope.** $V_L,V_R,V_C,v_b$ carry volts, $I,I_C,i_b$ amperes, $Q$ coulombs, $t$ seconds, $L$ henries ($\mathrm H=\mathrm V\,\mathrm s\,\mathrm A^{-1}$), $C$ farads ($\mathrm F=\mathrm C\,\mathrm V^{-1}$), and $R$ ohms ($\Omega=\mathrm V\,\mathrm A^{-1}$). The model excludes radiation, distributed-element, nonlinear, hysteretic, leakage and proximity effects; resistor loss is retained through $R$. Subluminal material speeds are required if a relativistic moving-matter interpretation is added. The model is adopted and contains no measurement or derivation from the vacuum Maxwell equations.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, let $x_0\in I$, and let $p,q:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. The IVP $y'+py=q$, $y(x_0)=y_0$, has exactly one solution on $I$, namely

$$y(x)=\exp(-P(x))\left(y_0+\int_{x_0}^x\exp(P(t))q(t)\,dt\right),\qquad P(x)=\int_{x_0}^x p(t)\,dt.$$

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and write $f=u+iv:U\to\mathbb C$. The following are equivalent:

1. $f$ is complex differentiable at $a$.
2. Under $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$, the map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and $Df(a)$ is multiplication by a complex number.
3. The map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and $\partial_{\bar z}f(a)=0$.
4. The map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations

$$ u_x(a)=v_y(a),\qquad u_y(a)=-v_x(a). $$

When these conditions hold,

$$ f'(a)=u_x(a)+iv_x(a)=v_y(a)-iu_y(a)=\partial_zf(a). $$

Let $f,g:U\to\mathbb C$ be complex differentiable at $a\in U$, and let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$. Then

$$ (\alpha f+\beta g)'(a)=\alpha f'(a)+\beta g'(a), $$

$$ (fg)'(a)=f'(a)g(a)+f(a)g'(a). $$

If $g(a)\ne0$, then $g$ is nonzero on some neighbourhood of $a$, the reciprocal $1/g$ is complex differentiable at $a$, and

$$ (1/g)'(a)=-\frac{g'(a)}{g(a)^2},\qquad (f/g)'(a)=\frac{f'(a)g(a)-f(a)g'(a)}{g(a)^2}. $$

Every constant function has derivative $0$, and the identity function has derivative $1$.

Let $f:U\to V$ and $g:V\to\mathbb C$, where $U,V\subseteq\mathbb C$ are open. If $f$ is complex differentiable at $a\in U$ and $g$ is complex differentiable at $f(a)$, then $g\circ f$ is complex differentiable at $a$ and

$$ (g\circ f)'(a)=g'(f(a))f'(a). $$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$
For every real $\theta$, $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

For every $z\in\mathbb C$,
$$\cos z=\cosh(iz),\qquad \sin z=-i\sinh(iz),\qquad \cosh z=\cos(iz),\qquad \sinh z=-i\sin(iz).$$
The complex functions restrict to their real sine, cosine, hyperbolic sine and hyperbolic cosine series on the real axis. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-functions]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]].

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Assume the lumped circuit model of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for clause (b), where it is inherited from the linkage suppliers.

(a) [Terminal-energy bookkeeping] Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval ([[def-interval]]), let $t_0,t_1\in J$, let $L\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be constant and symmetric, let $I:J\to\mathbb R^n$ be of class $C^1$ in the following sense: $I$ extends to a $C^1$ map on an open interval containing $J$, so that the derivatives used below are those of the extension (one-sided at included endpoints of $J$, and not intrinsic to a value restriction when $J$ is a singleton), and let $V(t):=L\dot I(t)$ be the terminal-voltage vector of the inductive branches as adopted in [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] (the Faraday branch: the terminal voltage of a branch is the rate of change of its flux linkage $\Phi=LI$). Then
$$\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\langle V(t),I(t)\rangle\,dt=\frac12\langle I(t_1),LI(t_1)\rangle-\frac12\langle I(t_0),LI(t_0)\rangle ,$$
and for $n=1$ with $L>0$ this reads $\int_{t_0}^{t_1}V I\,dt=\frac12L\bigl(I(t_1)^2-I(t_0)^2\bigr)$: the accumulated terminal energy equals the change of the inductor bookkeeping energy $\frac12LI^2$. The identity is exact for every such $C^1$ current and fixed geometry; it uses only symmetry of $L$, the product rule and the fundamental theorem of calculus. For a changing geometry the mechanical work done on the circuit is an additional term and is not covered here.

(b) [Identification with the frozen field energy] Suppose in addition that the currents are realized by fixed compact smooth conserved profiles $j_1,\dots,j_n$ of the class of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b), with instantaneous source $J_I(t):=\sum_\alpha I_\alpha(t)j_\alpha$, and that the inductance matrix is the linkage matrix of those profiles in the sense of [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]]: $L_{\alpha\beta}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\iint\frac{\langle j_\alpha(x),j_\beta(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x)$. Then for every $t\in J$
$$\frac12\langle I(t),LI(t)\rangle=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J_I(t),A_{J_I(t)}\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J_I(t)}|^2\,d\lambda_3\ \ge0,$$
where $A_{J_I(t)}$ is the Coulomb-gauge Newtonian vector potential and $B_{J_I(t)}=\operatorname{curl}A_{J_I(t)}$ of that theorem: the right-hand side is the magnetic field energy of the frozen instantaneous configuration, and the accumulated terminal energy of (a) between $t_0$ and $t_1$ is the change of this field energy. The relation $V=L\dot I$ is the explicitly adopted terminal law of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]]; the identification of the model's inductance matrix with the smooth-profile linkage matrix is part of the adopted model of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]].

(c) [Scope] no radiation, distributed-element, material-loss, moving-geometry or thin-wire self-inductance claim is made; the frozen-configuration energy is not asserted to be the energy of a time-dependent full Maxwell solution.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the cited unit-Dirichlet solvability and trace interfaces, and its Countable Choice consequence for surface and integral interfaces ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(\Omega;D_1,\dots,D_m;\Omega_v)$ be the conductor geometry of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]], additionally with $\Omega$ a bounded $C^\infty$ ambient domain and $\Omega_v$ connected and with the **outer boundary $\partial\Omega$ grounded**: the data on $\partial\Omega$ are the constant Dirichlet datum $0$; let $\rho_v\equiv0$ on $\Omega_v$ (the pure capacitor configuration: no volume source), and let the framework constants be those of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. For each $j\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ let $\varphi_j\in C^\infty(\overline{\Omega_v})$ be the unit-potential solution of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-existence]](c) with the smooth data
$$\varphi_j|_{\partial D_k}=\delta_{jk},\qquad \varphi_j|_{\partial\Omega}=0,$$
so that $-\Delta\varphi_j=0$ on $\Omega_v$ with the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], and let $\nu$ be the outward normal of $\Omega_v$ (so on $\partial D_j$ the normal $\nu$ points into the conductor). Define the **capacitance matrix** by
$$C_{jk}:=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}\frac{\partial\varphi_k}{\partial\nu}\,dS,\qquad j,k=1,\dots,m,$$
whose entries carry farads (F), with the unit potentials read as numerical volt values; these are flux integrals of continuous functions over the compact embedded hypersurfaces $\partial D_j$ (normal derivative of [[def-classical-normal-derivative]]) ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]]). Then:
(a) [Linearity and matrix form] for every $V=(V_1,\dots,V_m)\in\mathbb R^m$ the unique equilibrium potential with conductor potentials $V$ and grounded outer boundary is $\varphi^V=\sum_{j=1}^mV_j\varphi_j$, and the conductor charges of [[pthm-em-conductor-surface-charge]](d) are
$$Q_j(V)=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}\frac{\partial\varphi^V}{\partial\nu}\,dS=\sum_{k=1}^mC_{jk}V_k,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad Q=CV.$$
(b) [Reciprocity] $C$ is symmetric: $C_{jk}=C_{kj}$ for all $j,k$; the symmetry is Green's symmetric pairing of the harmonic potentials $\varphi_j,\varphi_k$.
(c) [Energy identity] the field energy of the configuration is
$$U(V)=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\Omega_v}|\nabla\varphi^V|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac12V^{T}CV=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^mV_jQ_j(V),$$
and $U(V)>0$ for every $V\ne0$: $C$ is symmetric positive definite. In particular $U(V)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $V=0$, so every nonzero conductor-potential data set stores positive field energy.
(d) [One driven terminal] with only conductor $1$ driven and every other conductor grounded, $V=te_1$, where $e_1:=(1,0,\ldots,0)\in\mathbb R^m$: $Q_1=C_{11}t$, $Q_j=C_{j1}t$ for $j\ne1$, and $U=\tfrac12C_{11}t^2=\tfrac12Q_1V_1=Q_1^2/(2C_{11})$; the **capacitance of the arrangement** at conductor $1$ with respect to the grounded reference is the positive geometric number $C_{11}>0$, with $C_{11}=Q_1/V_1$ when $t=V_1\ne0$, and the energy identities $U=\tfrac12QV=Q^2/(2C)=\tfrac12CV^2$ hold with $C=C_{11}$, $Q=Q_1$, $V=V_1$. By (c) the positivity holds for every diagonal entry, $C_{jj}>0$.
(e) [Assembly reading] use the family $V_j(s)=sV_j$, $\varphi_s=s\varphi^V$, $Q_j(s)=sQ_j(V)$ for $0\le s\le1$, with fixed geometry and grounded reference. Prescribe the quasistatic external charge-transfer work by $dW_{\rm ext}=\sum_jV_j(s)dQ_j(s)$. Then $W_{\rm ext}=\int_0^1s\,ds\sum_jV_jQ_j(V)=U$. The potentials vary during assembly; only the final potentials and geometry are fixed. This derives the sheet-charge accounting directly and does not apply the volume-source theorem [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]] to singular sheets. The family is an accounting prescription, not an asserted time-dependent Maxwell/material solution.
(f) [Scope] the theorem assumes: the compact separated conductor geometry, the additional bounded smooth ambient domain, and connected vacuum region of the model, the grounded outer boundary $\partial\Omega$, zero volume source, and the existence and uniqueness of the unit-potential Dirichlet solutions ([[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-existence]](c), [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-uniqueness]](a)). It asserts no solvability for arbitrary boundary data (the existence theorem is used only for the constant data above), no prescribed-total-charge problem, no dielectric or material response, no finite-conductivity or transient charging dynamics, no radiation, and no measurement; the matrix $C$ is a geometric object of the ideal electrostatic model, and infinite parallel planes require their own explicitly declared idealization, outside this bounded geometry.

derivations.claim: (a) Assume first that $J$ has at least two elements. Put $p:=R/L$, a constant of class $C^1$, and $q:=V/L$, continuous on $J$ by [F6]; $J$ is order-convex with at least two elements by [F2]. With $P(x):=\int_{t_0}^x p=\frac RL(x-t_0)$ one has $\exp(-P(x))=\exp\left(-\frac{R(x-t_0)}{L}\right)$ and $\exp(P(s))=\exp\left(\frac{R(s-t_0)}{L}\right)$, so the unique solution supplied by [F3] is exactly the displayed $I$. The ODE gives $\dot I=(V-RI)/L$, continuous on $J$. At each included finite endpoint extend $I$ to the outer side by the affine function with that endpoint value and slope; its derivative matches the one-sided ODE value, giving a $C^1$ extension to an open interval containing $J$. Its derivative on $J$ is the domain-relative derivative of [F4] (one-sided at included endpoints), and the uniqueness is the uniqueness assertion of [F3], which is the uniqueness of the $C^1$ solution in the sense of [F4]. If $J=\{t_0\}$, the restriction of any solution is $I_0$ by [F4]; choosing the constant extension $V\equiv V(t_0)$ on an open interval and applying the already-proved nondegenerate case there produces a $C^1$ extension of the candidate whose jet at $t_0$ is obtained by substituting $t=t_0$ into the differential equation, $\dot I(t_0)=(V(t_0)-RI_0)/L$, and no other extension is distinguished.

(b) Define the entire function $G(z):=z_0\exp(\mathrm i\Omega(z-t_0))$ on $\mathbb C$. By [F10] and [F11], applied to the affine map $z\mapsto \mathrm i\Omega(z-t_0)$ (derivative $\mathrm i\Omega$) and to [F8], $G$ is complex differentiable with $G'(z)=\mathrm i\Omega\,G(z)$ for every $z$; differentiating once more gives $G''=(\mathrm i\Omega)^2G=-\Omega^2G$. The function $w$ of the Statement is the restriction of $G$ to the real interval $J$, so by [F9] and the real chain rule [F12] it is real differentiable with $w'(t)=\mathrm i\Omega\,w(t)$ and $w''(t)=-\Omega^2w(t)$ for every $t\in J$; taking real parts, $Q=\operatorname{Re}w$ is of class $C^2$ with $Q'(t)=\operatorname{Re}w'(t)$ and $Q''(t)=\operatorname{Re}w''(t)$, because the real part is real-linear. Hence $Q''=-\Omega^2Q$, which is $LQ''+Q/C=0$ since $\Omega^2=1/(LC)$ by definition. At $t_0$: $w(t_0)=z_0$ gives $Q(t_0)=\operatorname{Re}z_0=Q_0$, and $w'(t_0)=\mathrm i\Omega z_0=\mathrm i\Omega Q_0+I_0$ gives $Q'(t_0)=I_0$. Euler's formula [F13] expands $\exp(\mathrm i\Omega(t-t_0))=\cos\Omega(t-t_0)+\mathrm i\sin\Omega(t-t_0)$, and multiplying out $w=z_0\exp(\mathrm i\Omega(t-t_0))$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=Q_0\cos\Omega(t-t_0)+(I_0/\Omega)\sin\Omega(t-t_0)$, with the real trigonometric functions of [F13] and the real restriction recorded in [F14]. For $J=\{t_0\}$ the same formulas are evaluated at $t_0$, the entire function supplying the jets $\dot Q(t_0)=I_0$ and $\ddot Q(t_0)=-\Omega^2Q_0=-Q_0/(LC)$ by the same computation, so the LC candidate needs no separate singleton convention.

(a) Along the solution of step 1.1 the function $t\mapsto\frac12LI(t)^2$ is differentiable at every interior point of $J$ (and one-sidedly at included endpoints) by [F5], with derivative $LI\dot I$; substituting the circuit equation $L\dot I=V-RI$ gives $LI\dot I=VI-RI^2$, which is the power identity.

(b) Define $E(t):=\frac12LQ'(t)^2+\frac{Q(t)^2}{2C}$; by [F6] and step 1.2 the functions $Q$ and $Q'$ are continuous, so $E$ is continuous on $J$, and at every interior point of $J$ the product and scalar rules of [F5] give $E'=LQ'Q''+QQ'/C=Q'(LQ''+Q/C)=0$ by the equation of step 1.2. By [F15], $E$ is constant on $J$, and its value is $E(t_0)=\frac12LI_0^2+\frac{Q_0^2}{2C}$ by the initial values of step 1.2. The first summand is the inductive bookkeeping energy of [F16], and for the optional geometric identification of the Statement the second summand is the frozen electrostatic field energy supplied by the declared clause of [L1] under full AC and the stated conductor arrangement, with $C=C_{11}$ and $V_1=Q/C_{11}$; the magnetic realization of the inductive term is the separate smooth-profile clause of [F16], under its $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ premise. For $J=\{t_0\}$ the constant-energy display is the value at $t_0$ supplied by step 1.2, so no derivative of a singleton restriction is used.

The full choice hypothesis of the geometric identification is [A1], and the inductive realization of [F16] carries the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [A2]; full AC yields it, because for a sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets the family $\{X_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ of its values consists of nonempty sets, so [A1] provides a choice function $g$ on that family and $n\mapsto g(X_n)$ is a choice function for the sequence, as [A2] requires. Hence clause (b) is available under its stated hypotheses, and the RL and LC algebra of steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2 is choice-free and uses neither [A1] nor [A2].

Clauses (a)-(c) are established: step 1.1 and step 2.1 give the existence, uniqueness, formula and power identity of (a); step 1.2 and step 2.2 give the solution, initial values, cosine-sine form, energy identity and conservation of (b), with the geometric identification delegated to [L1]; step 3.1 accounts for the choice use. The units are [F17]; no general network completeness, no full time-dependent Maxwell solution, no radiation or distributed-element effect and no empirical claim is asserted, and both statements are consequences of the expressly adopted relations of [F1].

boundaries.evidence: The hypothesis $t_0\in J$ excludes an empty interval; if $J=\{t_0\}$ the singleton clauses of steps 1.1 and 1.2 apply, and step 2.2 reads the constant energy at $t_0$.

For $R=0$ step 1.1 reduces the formula to $I_0+L^{-1}\int_{t_0}^tV$; for $I_0=0$ and $V\equiv0$ it gives $I\equiv0$ and the power identity $0=0$; for $Q_0=I_0=0$ step 1.2 gives $w\equiv0$ and step 2.2 gives $E\equiv0$.
No counting parameter occurs: the LC frequency is the single number $\Omega=(LC)^{-1/2}>0$ of step 1.2, fixed by the product $LC$ alone, and the RL coefficient is the single ratio $R/L$.

For $J=\{t_0\}$ step 1.1 gives the restriction $I_0$ and the canonical-extension jet $(V(t_0)-RI_0)/L$ without asserting a derivative of the singleton restriction, and step 1.2 gives the LC jets $\dot Q=I_0$, $\ddot Q=-Q_0/(LC)$ from the entire candidate.

For nondegenerate $J$ the derivatives are domain-relative with one-sided values at included endpoints in the sense of [F4], and step 1.1 applies [F3] on $J$; the open-neighbourhood extension of the Statement supplies the endpoint jets and step 2.2 differentiates only at interior points, as [F15] requires. Step 1.1 uses continuous derivative (V-RI)/L and affine continuations on the outer side of included endpoints to construct the stated C1 open-neighbourhood extension.

The RL solution, the LC candidate and the energy algebra of steps 1.1-2.2 are choice-free as the Statement declares; full AC enters only through [L1]'s geometric capacitor identification in step 2.2, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ only through [F16]'s smooth-profile realization, with step 3.1 deriving the latter from the former.
The item asserts no if-and-only-if of its own; the energy conservation of step 2.2 is an equality of functions, and the equivalence $U(I)=0\iff J_I=0$ used through [F16] is quoted from its supplier.
There is no converse direction to discharge: step 2.2 proves $E'\equiv0$ and hence constancy, and does not claim that constant energy forces the LC equation, which is separately verified in step 1.2.
